We analysed the interactions between the V 2R phosphopeptide (V2Rpp) and β-arrestins-1 and 2, mimicking the tail-only engaged receptor-arrestin conformation. Interaction of V 2Rpp with β-arrestins labelled with mBBr (monobromobimane) in the finger loop results in an increase in fluorescence intensity. This suggests the disruption of the ionic lock and the release of the finger-loop. We then analysed the interactions between β-arrestins-1 and 2 with the active (agonist-bound) and phosphorylated receptor ( β2V2R – a chimeric β2-adrenergic receptor that harbours the V 2R tail). We determined the residue contact networks (RCNs, Methods) of 18 arrestin structures. Together, all residue contacts of a particular protein structure represent a ‘contact fingerprint’ typical for that protein and its conformation 24,26. Clustering protein structures by their ‘contact fingerprints’ allows for an unbiased classification of distinct conformational states. The arrestin structures cluster into two major groups: inactive state (13 structures, Methods) and active state (5 structures). Within the cluster of active-state structures, the V2Rpp (vasopressin-2 receptor phosphopeptide) 14 bound arrestin forms a sub-cluster with the inositol hexakisphosphate-bound arrestin 27. The fact that these two structures appear to have similar contact fingerprints suggests that the phosphorylation-dependent mechanism of arrestin activation is conserved irrespective of the source of phosphates.

We find that 17 of 19 arrestin positions that interact with receptor attached phosphates and 22 of 27 interface residues that interact with the receptor helix bundle are identical between human and tiger salamander cone arrestin. Thus, the identified motifs is conserved even in more distantly related receptor-arrestin interactions. Consensus RCNs— To generate the consensus RCNs, only contacts that are present in all chains of a particular structure were considered. Subsequently, for each signaling state, contacts that were present in all structures in the particular signaling state were defined as consensus contacts. These two filtering steps help to increase stringency of the contact definition and reduce noise from contact networks.

This information is stored as a bit string of ones (present) and zeros (absent), which are referred to here as ‘contact fingerprints’. Identifying contact fingerprints that represent consistently maintained residues contacts across and between conformational states enabled us to identify conserved rearrangement of residue contacts in class A GPCRs. For the identification of residue contacts that are specific either to the inactive or the active states, we focused only on the GPCRs that had structures determined in both inactive as well as active state. For the analysis of contacts across GPCRs including the inactive and active state only structures (Fig. 4b), the contact distance threshold was computed based on the sum of the van der Waals radii of atoms plus multiple cut-off distance between 0.5 and 0.8 Å, in order to account for variation in the quality of structures. These ﬁndings reinforce the idea that the nature of amino acid properties at the selectivity bar code region on the G a-binding interface of the RGS protein comprises major determinants of G arecognition selectivity. Design Principles for Engineering RGS Protein Selectivity The identiﬁcation of selectivity bar code residues in RGS pro- teins raises a question about their necessity and sufﬁciency insetting the selectivity of G arecognition. This question was ad- dressed experimentally, by transplanting the entire distributed pattern of selectivity residues ( Figure 6 A). For these experiments, we chose RGS13 and RGS18, which belong to the same R4 sub- family but differ in G protein selectivity ( Figure 6 C). RGS13 pre- fers G qmembers over the G i/osubfamily, whereas RGS18 equally regulates both G i/oand G qproteins.

Discussion The objective of this study was to demonstrate the feasibility and potential of our innovative DCyFIR platform. Using this tech- nology, we have identified a relatively large number of GPCR – ligand interactions by profiling a relatively small number of com- pounds and receptors. These discoveries are solely attributable to the multiplex format of the DCyFIR experiment, which enablessimultaneous ligand profiling of many GPCRs at once. In the discussion that follows, we characterize a select number of our findings in the context of their potential biological relevance. Interactions between GPCRs and Amino Acid Metabolites. In this work we showed that the DCyFIR platform can be used to identify interactions between GPCRs and small molecule regu-lators. For example, we identified several GPCR –ligand inter- actions involving three amino acid metabolites that belong to the tryptophan pathway: KYNA, serotonin, and tryptamine.

By combining the scalability of a yeast-strainreceptor plex with the low requirement for ligand material, it is highly practical to expand our many-GPCR versus many-ligand format to entire compound libraries, as we have demonstratedfor human metabolites, effectively screening hundreds of GPCR –Gα combinations versus hundreds (or thousands) of ligands at once. More traditional GPCR assays that use readouts such as secondmessengers, β-arrestin recruitment, and BRET have tremendous value, but are much more resource intensive (and likely cost prohibitive), both in terms of the amounts of transfected cells andligands required. The DCyFIR platform serves to lower these barriers. In conclusion, we have demonstrated the utility of the DCy- FIR platform for simultaneously profiling many GPCRs against individual ligands to efficiently explore chemical space. We haveestablished that this innovative approach facilitates the rapid,inexpensive, and comprehensive assessment of ligand specificity and receptor promiscuity. We believe that combining the DCy- FIR platform with other GPCR screening approaches has thepotential to open avenues in GPCR research.

We used Foldseek commit aeb5e dur - ing this analysis. We expose Foldseek-TM in our command-line interface as a search mode that combines regular Foldseek 3Di/AA-based work - flow with our TM-align implementation within the tmalign module. MMseqs2 We used the default MMseqs2 (release 13-45111) search algorithm to obtain the sequence-based alignment result. MMseqs2 sorts the results by E value and score. We searched with: --threads 64 -s 7.5 -e 10000 --max-seqs 2000. CLE-Smith–Waterman We used PDB Tool version 4.80 ( https://github.com/realbigws/ PDB_Tool) to convert the benchmark structure set to CLE sequences. After the conversion, we used SSW35 (commit ad452e) to align CLE sequences all-versus-all. We sorted the results by alignment score.

To remove sources of variation that are unique to one of the data sets and align the cell line and tumor data we used a multi-step process. First, we used contrastive principal component analysis (cPCA)37to identify correlated variability that is enriched in the tumor data compared to the cell line data, or vice-versa. In order to avoid identifying signatures related to differences in the cancer type or subtype compositions of the datasets we ﬁrst clustered the tumor and cell line data separately and subtracted the average expression of each cluster from allsamples in the cluster to estimate the average intra-cluster covariance for tumors and cell lines. The data sets were clustered in 70-dimensional PCA space using a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) based clustering method implemented in the SeuratR package 73, with a resolution parameter of 5. We then regressed out the ﬁrst four cPCs (components which had higher variance in the tumor data) from both the tumor and cell line data

CONCLUSION: Our data demonstrate that the detection and structural characterization of the distinct conformational states populated by a kinase, coupled to the energetic dissection of the contribution of key structural elements to the selective stability of these states, areessential to advance our understanding of the mechanisms underpinning kinase regulation and function. The other transductive approaches are either completely inappropriate in an inductive setting or assume that nodes are incrementally added to a single graph, making them unusable for the setup where test graphs are completely unseen during training (such as the PPI dataset). Additionally, for both tasks we provide the performance of a per-node shared multilayer perceptron (MLP) classiﬁer (that does not incorporate graph structure at all). 3.3 E XPERIMENTAL SETUP Transductive learning For the transductive learning tasks, we apply a two-layer GAT model. Its architectural hyperparameters have been optimized on the Cora dataset and are then reused for Cite- seer.

We overcome this with a hardware-aware algorithm that exploits the memory hierarchy on modern hardware (Section 3.3). We then describe a simple SSM architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (Section 3.4). Finally, we discuss some additional properties of selection mechanisms (Section 3.5). 3.1 Motivation: Selection as a Means of Compression We argue that a fundamental problem of sequence modeling is compressing context into a smaller state. In fact, we can view the tradeoﬀs of popular sequence models from this point of view. For example, attention is both eﬀective and ineﬃcient because it explicitly does not compress context at all. This can be seen from the fact that autoregressive inference requires explicitly storing the entire context (i.e. the KV cache), which directly causes the slow linear-time inference and quadratic-time training of Transformers. On the other hand, recurrent models are eﬃcient because they have a ﬁnite state, implying constant-time inference and linear-time training.

•Replacing the complex-valued S4 variant from previous work with a real-valued one does not aﬀect performance much, suggesting that (at least for LM) real-valued SSMs may be a better choice when accounting for hardware eﬃciency. •Replacing any of these with a selective SSM (S6) signiﬁcantly improves performance, validating the motivation of Section 3. •The Mamba architecture performs similarly to the H3 architecture (and seems slightly better when using a selective layer). Even though we trained only on cocrystallized protein complexes, we also tested our method in a benchmark set of 40 proteins crystal - lized in the unbound (apo) state. Since unbound docking is substan - tially more challenging, we changed the success criteria to finding the correct complex within the top 1,000, top 100 and top ten, for all methods (Table 2). Here the performance of all tools deterio - rates, with slightly better accuracy for ZDock and ZDock+ZRank2. Although MaSIF-search can recover many of the complexes in the top 1,000 results, the scoring neural network, which was trained on holo structures, does not rank these into the top ten. These results point to the need for training MaSIF on apo structures, perhaps by augmenting datasets with simulated unbound states.

388 | CANCER DISCOVERY APRIL 2013 www.aacrjournals.org REVIEW The Basic Principles of Chimeric Antigen Receptor Design Michel Sadelain , Renier Brentjens , and Isabelle Rivière ABSTRACT Chimeric antigen receptors (CAR) are recombinant receptors that provide both antigen-binding and T-cell–activating functions. A multitude of CARs has been reported over the past decade, targeting an array of cell surface tumor antigens. Their biologic functions have dramatically changed following the introduction of tripartite receptors comprising a costimulatory domain, termed second-generation CARs. These have recently shown clinical beneﬁ t in patients treated with CD19-targeted autologous T cells. CARs may be combined with costimulatory ligands, chimeric costimulatory receptors, or cytokines to further enhance T-cell potency, speciﬁ city, and safety.

Majzner1,3,5 ✉ Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have altered the treatment landscape for B cell malignancies, the risk of on-target, off-tumour toxicity has hampered their development for solid tumours because most target antigens are shared with normal cells1,2. Researchers have attempted to apply Boolean-logic gating to CAR T cells to prevent toxicity3–5; however, a truly safe and effective logic-gated CAR has remained elusive6.

514 | Nature | Vol 615 | 16 March 2023 ArticleLINK outperforms other logic-gated CARs There have been several previous attempts in the literature to generate AND-gate CAR T cells. These include a ‘SPLIT’ CAR system, in which the CD3ζ and costimulatory domains are split into CARs with different spe - cificities3, as well as gene circuits such as the SynNotch system4. In the SynNotch system, in response to encounter of a first antigen (antigen A), a synthetic Notch receptor releases a transcription factor that then drives the expression of a traditional cytolytic CAR with specificity for a second antigen (antigen B). Thus, SynNotch cells are primed by antigen A to recognize and kill cells that express antigen B. Although this system is designed to program transcriptional responses in T cells, it is not a true AND gate because cells that are primed by antigen A can then attack any tissue expressing antigen B (Extended Data Fig. 10a).

Since it is generally assumedthat the function of a protein is closely linked to its three-dimensionalstructure, prediction or experimental determination of the library of pro-tein structures is a matter of high priority. However, a large proportionof gene sequences appear to code not for folded, globular proteins, butfor long stretches of amino acids that are likely to be either unfolded insolution or adopt non-globular structures of unknown conformation.Characterization of the conformational propensities and function of thenon-globular protein sequences represents a major challenge.

NATURE REVIEWS |MOLECULAR CELL BIOLOGY VOLUME 6 |MARCH 2005 |205REVIEWS More roles for intrinsically disordered proteins An in-depth examination of all of the examples of functional unfolded proteins in processes such as tran- scription, translation, signal transduction and cell-cycle control will have to form the subject of a different review. However, to conclude this review, we survey a few areas in which intrinsically unstructured proteins have been found to have important roles. Protein–nucleic-acid recognition. DNA-binding pro- teins seem to have evolved an ingenious array of tech- niques for dealing with the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of binding to specific DNA sequences, and many of them involve the use of unfolded or partly folded proteins. A role for induced protein folding in sequence-specific DNA binding was proposed more than a decade ago by Spolar and Record108,on the basis of the large heat-capacity changes that result from DNA–protein complex formation.

NATURE REVIEWS |MOLECULAR CELL BIOLOGY VOLUME 6 |MARCH 2005 |205REVIEWS More roles for intrinsically disordered proteins An in-depth examination of all of the examples of functional unfolded proteins in processes such as tran- scription, translation, signal transduction and cell-cycle control will have to form the subject of a different review. However, to conclude this review, we survey a few areas in which intrinsically unstructured proteins have been found to have important roles. Protein–nucleic-acid recognition. DNA-binding pro- teins seem to have evolved an ingenious array of tech- niques for dealing with the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of binding to specific DNA sequences, and many of them involve the use of unfolded or partly folded proteins. A role for induced protein folding in sequence-specific DNA binding was proposed more than a decade ago by Spolar and Record108,on the basis of the large heat-capacity changes that result from DNA–protein complex formation.

However, to conclude this review, we survey a few areas in which intrinsically unstructured proteins have been found to have important roles. Protein–nucleic-acid recognition. DNA-binding pro- teins seem to have evolved an ingenious array of tech- niques for dealing with the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of binding to specific DNA sequences, and many of them involve the use of unfolded or partly folded proteins. A role for induced protein folding in sequence-specific DNA binding was proposed more than a decade ago by Spolar and Record108,on the basis of the large heat-capacity changes that result from DNA–protein complex formation.

However, to conclude this review, we survey a few areas in which intrinsically unstructured proteins have been found to have important roles. Protein–nucleic-acid recognition. DNA-binding pro- teins seem to have evolved an ingenious array of tech- niques for dealing with the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of binding to specific DNA sequences, and many of them involve the use of unfolded or partly folded proteins. A role for induced protein folding in sequence-specific DNA binding was proposed more than a decade ago by Spolar and Record108,on the basis of the large heat-capacity changes that result from DNA–protein complex formation.

For example, we find that some functions— such as DNA-binding ability, or localization in nuclear speckles—are enriched in proteins that have compact IDRs, whereas components of mitochondria and endosomes are enriched in expanded IDRs. Our large sequence–ensemble dataset reveals the sequence properties that determine conformational ensembles, including the interplay between overall hydrophobicity and charge patterning. We take advantage of this knowledge and our ensembles to train a machine-learning model to predict protein compaction from sequence only, and use it to show that IDRs in orthologues of human proteins have conserved conforma - tional properties. In a cellular context, many IDRs form interactions with other molecules, and chain compaction and charge properties of the monomer quantify key aspects of a protein’s ability to form both intra- and intermolecular interactions.

Johansson1 & Kresten Lindorff-Larsen1 ✉ Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (collectively, IDRs) are pervasive across proteomes in all kingdoms of life, help to shape biological functions and are involved in numerous diseases. IDRs populate a diverse set of transiently formed structures and defy conventional sequence–structure–function relationships1. Developments in protein science have made it possible to predict the three-dimensional structures of folded proteins at the proteome scale2.

ARE THERE AC(ET)YL-LYSINE READER DOMAINS IN BACTERIA? In eukaryotes next to the lysine ac(et)yltransferases (writers) and deac(et)ylases (erasers) also reader domains for ac(et)yl lysine were reported. These were the bromodomains (BRDs) and theYEATS (Y af9, ENL, AF9, Taf14, Sas5) domains. Bromodomains were ﬁrst identiﬁed in the protein Brahma in Drosophila (Tamkun et al., 1992). This protein is part of a multi-protein complex involved in chromatin remodeling. Today it is known that BRDs are speciﬁc acetyl-L-lysine binding domains composed of approximately 110 residues forming an unusual left-handed four-helix bundle (Dhalluin et al., 1999; Mujtaba et al., 2007). The binding site of the acetyl-L-Lysine is a hydrophobic cavity formed by loops connecting the α-helices.

This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license (https:// creativecommons.org/licenses/by/ 4.0/).Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Semmelweis University, 1094 Budapest, Hungary; chinopoulos.christos@eok.sote.hu; Tel.: +36-1-459-1500 (ext. 60024); Fax: +36-1-267-0031 Abstract: Lysine succinylation is a post-translational modiﬁcation which alters protein function in both physiological and pathological processes. Mindful that it requires succinyl-CoA, a metabolite formed within the mitochondrial matrix that cannot permeate the inner mitochondrial membrane, the question arises as to how there can be succinylation of proteins outside mitochondria. The present mini-review examines pathways participating in peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation that lead to succinyl-CoA production, potentially supporting succinylation of extramitochondrial proteins. Furthermore, the inﬂuence of the mitochondrial status on cytosolic NAD+availability affecting the activity of cytosolic SIRT5 iso1 and iso4—in turn regulating cytosolic protein lysine succinylations—is presented.

Yes, despite the diversity among G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), there are similarities in their activation pathways. The study you referenced identifies key similarities that converge near the G-protein-coupling region of these receptors. Here are the main points:

Converging Activation Pathways: While GPCRs are diverse in their structures and the types of ligands they bind, their activation pathways show a significant convergence near the region where the receptors couple with G proteins.

Conserved Structural Rearrangement: A highly conserved structural rearrangement of residue contacts between transmembrane helices 3, 6, and 7 has been observed. This rearrangement is critical in facilitating the release of residues that contact G proteins, leading to receptor activation.

Functional Implication: The convergence of these activation pathways near the G-protein-coupling region suggests that despite the variety in initial activation steps (triggered by diverse ligands), there is a common mechanism by which these receptors ultimately interact with G proteins. This commonality helps explain how different GPCRs can bind to and activate a shared set of G proteins.

In summary, while the initial activation steps of GPCRs may differ due to their diverse ligands and structural variations, the pathways converge at a critical point near the G-protein-coupling region through conserved structural rearrangements. This convergence is essential for the uniform activation of G proteins across different GPCRs.

Conserved Structural Rearrangement: A highly conserved structural rearrangement of residue contacts between transmembrane helices 3, 6, and 7 has been observed. This rearrangement is critical in facilitating the release of residues that contact G proteins, leading to receptor activation.

Conserved Residues: The residues that participate in the activation pathways of GPCRs, especially those near the G-protein-coupling region, tend to be highly conserved across different receptors. This conservation highlights their critical role in the activation process.

Structural Elements: These conserved residues are part of specific structural elements within the GPCRs, particularly the transmembrane helices. The study you referenced specifically mentions transmembrane helices 3, 6, and 7 as being crucial for these structural rearrangements.

Yes, according to the study by Venkatakrishnan et al. (2017), there are significant rearrangements in the process of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) activation. The study used a combination of structural biology and bioinformatics techniques to investigate the conformational changes that occur in GPCRs upon activation.

The authors found that the activation of GPCRs involves a conserved rearrangement of residue contacts between the inactive and active state structures. Specifically, they identified 117 contacts that are only present in the inactive state, 61 contacts that are only present in the active, G protein-bound state, and 191 contacts that are present in both the inactive and active states.

Furthermore, the study showed that the rearrangement of residue contacts involves a movement of helices 6 and 7 upon activation, which is conserved across diverse class A GPCRs. This movement is thought to facilitate the binding of G protein and the activation of downstream signaling pathways.

Overall, the study demonstrates that the process of GPCR activation involves significant conformational changes in the receptor structure, which are conserved across different GPCRs and are likely to be important for their function.

The activation mechanism of arrestins and how different patterns of receptor phosphorylation induce distinct conformational changes in arrestins involve several key steps and molecular interactions. Here's a detailed explanation:

Receptor Phosphorylation:

GPCRs are phosphorylated by G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) on their intracellular domains, primarily the C-terminal tail and the third intracellular loop.
The pattern and extent of phosphorylation (often referred to as the "phosphorylation barcode") vary depending on the specific receptor and the type of ligand that activates the receptor.
Phosphorylation Barcode:

The specific pattern of phosphorylation sites on the receptor acts as a barcode, which is recognized by different regions on arrestins.
This barcode influences the conformation that arrestin adopts when it binds to the phosphorylated receptor.
Binding and Conformational Changes:

When arrestin binds to a phosphorylated GPCR, it undergoes significant conformational changes.
These changes are initiated by the interaction between phosphorylated residues on the receptor and specific domains in arrestin, including the N-domain, C-domain, and inter-domain hinge regions.
Structural Motifs in Arrestin:

A conserved structural motif in arrestin restricts the mobility of the finger loop in the inactive state.
Phosphorylation of the receptor releases this restriction by engaging with specific sites on arrestin, causing the finger loop and other structural elements to shift.
These shifts allow arrestin to transition from an inactive to an active conformation capable of binding to the receptor and downstream signaling proteins.
Micro-locks and Finger Loop:

Arrestin contains several structural motifs, termed "micro-locks," which are selectively engaged by different receptor phosphorylation sites.
Distal and proximal phosphorylation sites on the receptor differentially engage these micro-locks, inducing specific conformational changes in arrestin.
The finger loop, a critical region for arrestin activation, undergoes conformational rearrangement depending on how the micro-locks are engaged.

Arrestin activation is primarily triggered by the phosphorylation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) by G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs). Upon ligand binding, activated GPCRs recruit GRKs, which phosphorylate specific serine and threonine residues on the receptor's intracellular domains. This phosphorylation creates binding sites for arrestins. The binding of arrestins to phosphorylated GPCRs induces a conformational change in arrestins, transitioning them from an inactive to an active state. This activation process involves the rearrangement of arrestin domains, particularly the movement of the C-terminal tail and the disruption of the polar core region.

Different patterns of receptor phosphorylation can induce distinct conformational changes in arrestins due to the differential recruitment and binding of arrestin isoforms. Each arrestin isoform has unique structural features that dictate its interactions with phosphorylated receptors. Variations in the number and arrangement of phosphorylated residues on the receptor's intracellular domains influence the binding affinity and orientation of arrestins, leading to diverse conformational changes. These conformational changes not only determine the affinity of arrestins for GPCRs but also govern their ability to engage downstream signaling partners and regulate various cellular responses, including receptor desensitization, internalization, and alternative signaling pathway activation. Thus, the interplay between receptor phosphorylation patterns and arrestin conformational dynamics contributes to the specificity and versatility of arrestin-mediated signaling.

C-terminal Tail: The cytoplasmic C-terminal tail of GPCRs is a major site for phosphorylation. This region often contains multiple serine and threonine residues that can be phosphorylated by G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) and other kinases.

Third Intracellular Loop: The third intracellular loop (ICL3) is another critical region that undergoes phosphorylation. Like the C-terminal tail, it contains serine and threonine residues that are accessible to kinases.

Phosphorylated sites on the receptor tail act like recognition tags for arrestins. These negatively charged phosphate groups interact with positively charged pockets on the surface of arrestins.  While the specific sequence of phosphorylated residues can vary,  arrestins contain conserved clusters of positively charged amino acids that serve as general phosphate sensors.  Imagine the phospho-sites as bumps on a key, fitting into designated grooves (conserved charged pockets) on the arrestin surface.  This interaction triggers a conformational change in arrestin, but the specific details of the shift depend on the exact number, spacing, and location of the phosphorylated residues.  In essence, the interplay between conserved arrestin pockets and the unique phospho-barcode dictates the tailored fit and function of arrestin in the signaling pathway.

Definition:

A selectivity barcode refers to distinct patterns of amino acids on G proteins that are recognized by specific regions on GPCRs. These patterns allow for selective binding and activation of G proteins by their corresponding receptors.
Universally Conserved Positions:

Certain positions within the G-protein barcode are universally conserved across different G proteins. These conserved residues enable a basic level of interaction necessary for the binding and activation of G proteins by GPCRs.
Unique Positions:

In addition to the conserved residues, there are unique positions within the barcode that vary among different G proteins. These unique residues are responsible for the specific recognition by different GPCRs, allowing for selective coupling.

Universally Conserved Residue Positions in G Proteins
P-loop (Phosphate-binding loop) / Walker A Motif:

Glycine (G): Typically found in the P-loop, glycine residues contribute to the flexibility needed for binding GDP and GTP.
Lysine (K): Often located within the P-loop, this residue is essential for coordinating the phosphate groups of the nucleotide.
Example: Glycine at position 60 (Gly60) in G_ subunits.
Switch I Region:

Threonine (T) or Serine (S): These residues interact with the phosphate groups of GTP, playing a critical role in the conformational changes during GTP binding and hydrolysis.
Example: Threonine at position 35 (Thr35) in G_ subunits.
Switch II Region:

Aspartate (D): Part of the DXXG motif, which is crucial for GTP hydrolysis.
Glycine (G): Within the DXXG motif, providing flexibility for the switch region movements.
Example: Aspartate at position 136 (Asp136) in G_ subunits.
Switch III Region:

Hydrophobic Residues: Residues like leucine (L) or isoleucine (I) that help maintain the structural integrity during activation.
Example: Conserved hydrophobic residues in this region can vary, but are generally present to stabilize the structure.
Nucleotide Binding Site (Walker B Motif):

Magnesium Ion Coordinating Residues: Typically involves a conserved aspartate (D) or glutamate (E) that coordinates the magnesium ion required for nucleotide binding.
Example: Aspartate residues involved in coordinating Mg2+ in the nucleotide-binding pocket.
GTPase Domain:

Glutamine (Q): Important for catalyzing the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP.
Example: Glutamine at position 61 (Gln61) in G_ subunits.
Functional Importance
Structural Integrity: Conserved residues ensure the G protein maintains its correct folding and stability.
Nucleotide Binding and Hydrolysis: These residues are directly involved in binding GDP/GTP and catalyzing the hydrolysis of GTP, which is critical for the G protein's role as a molecular switch.
Interaction with GPCRs and Effectors: Conserved residues facilitate the interaction between G proteins and their respective GPCRs and downstream effectors, ensuring accurate signal transduction.
Examples of Specific Universally Conserved Residues in G_ Subunits
Gly60: Located in the P-loop, essential for phosphate binding.
Thr35: Located in Switch I, interacts with the _-phosphate of GTP.
Asp136: Located in Switch II, part of the DXXG motif crucial for GTP hydrolysis.
Gln61: Located in the GTPase domain, catalyzes GTP hydrolysis.

Recognition Mechanism
Structural Complementarity:

Intracellular Loops (ICLs): The intracellular loops of GPCRs, particularly ICL2 and ICL3, interact directly with the Î±5 helix and other regions of the G protein.
C-terminal Tail of GPCRs: This region can also engage with G proteins, adding another layer of specificity.
Amino Acid Interactions:

Conserved Residues: Universally conserved residues in both the GPCR and the G protein ensure a basic level of interaction necessary for coupling.
Variable Residues: Unique residues in the G-protein barcode and the corresponding binding sites on GPCRs contribute to the specificity of the interaction. These residues interact through hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic bonds.

The overall model for the GPCR-G protein interaction selectivities, as proposed by Flock et al. (2018) in their study published in Nature, suggests that GPCRs recognize and bind to specific G proteins through a conserved mechanism. The same G protein can be activated by different receptors, and the same receptor can couple to different G proteins. This interaction is mediated by the binding of the receptor to the G protein through a specific interface.

The study used a combination of sequence and structure-derived information to understand how GPCRs read the G protein selectivity barcode, which is a specific sequence pattern on the G protein that determines its binding preferences. The authors found that the G protein selectivity barcode is mapped onto the GPCR-G protein interface clusters obtained using the _2AR-Gs complex structure. This integration of sequence and structure-derived information highlights which regions of the GPCR contact selectivity-determining residues on the G protein, providing insight into how GPCRs recognize and bind to specific G proteins.

The overall model suggests that GPCRs have evolved to recognize and bind to specific G proteins through a precise binding mechanism, which is determined by the sequence of the receptor and the structure of the G protein. This mechanism allows for the selective activation of different G proteins by different receptors, leading to complex signaling pathways and networks.

The existence of a strict "selectivity barcode" in Regulators of G protein Signaling (RGS) proteins for G protein binding is not as well-established as in G proteins themselves. However, RGS proteins exhibit selectivity in their interactions with G protein subtypes, primarily mediated by conserved structural features within the RGS domain.

The RGS domain contains key residues crucial for binding to activated G_ subunits and accelerating their GTP hydrolysis. While not organized in a barcode-like pattern, these residues contribute to the specificity of RGS-G protein interactions. Specificity is also influenced by variations in the RGS domain sequence and structure among different RGS proteins, leading to preferential binding to certain G protein subtypes.

Furthermore, auxiliary domains or protein-protein interaction motifs outside the RGS domain may also modulate selectivity. While the concept of a "selectivity barcode" in RGS proteins is less defined, the combined effects of conserved residues, structural motifs, and domain variations contribute to the specificity observed in RGS-G protein interactions. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for unraveling the complexities of G protein signaling regulation and developing targeted therapeutic interventions.

The structural preference for selectivity barcode residues in RGS proteins involves specific variable residues in the Î±4-Î±5 loop, Î±7 helix, and other regions of the RGS domain that interact with distinct regions of GÎ± subunits. These residues form specific hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, and hydrophobic contacts, contributing to the selective binding and efficient GTPase activation of particular GÎ± subunits.

According to the study by Masuho et al. (2017), non-synonymous variants in the selectivity barcodes of RGS proteins can have a significant impact on G protein signaling. The authors identified 23 non-synonymous variants in the selectivity barcodes of 14 RGS proteins and investigated their effect on G protein recognition. They found that these variants altered the G protein preferences of the RGS proteins, resulting in different GAP activity profiles.

The study used a global map of G protein signaling regulation by RGS proteins to systematically analyze the impact of non-synonymous variants in the selectivity barcodes of RGS proteins on G protein recognition. The authors found that these variants could either enhance or diminish the GAP activity of the RGS proteins, leading to changes in their G protein preferences.

The study also demonstrated that the mutational genomic landscape can shape the RGS selectivity, and the authors showed that individual residues within the bar code can have an impact on the G protein selectivity of RGS proteins. Furthermore, they found that altering these determinants can generate RGS proteins with novel selectivity pro-files not displayed by canonical members of the family.

Overall, the study suggests that non-synonymous variants in the selectivity barcodes of RGS proteins can have a significant impact on G protein signaling and can lead to the creation of new RGS proteins with different G protein preferences. These findings have implications for pharmacogenomics and understanding disease mechanisms associated with the disruption in RGS-mediated G protein control.

Based on the provided references, the overall mechanism for RGS-Galpha-based signaling involves several steps:

1. G protein alpha subunits (Galpha) bind to specific ligands at the cell surface, triggering a conformational change that activates the Galpha subunit.
2. Activated Galpha subunits interact with and release RGS proteins (RGS7, RGS14, etc.) from their inhibitory binding sites.
3. RGS proteins then bind to and inhibit the activity of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), thereby preventing the activation of downstream signaling pathways.
4. The interaction between Galpha and RGS proteins is mediated by specific domains on both proteins, including the Galpha C-terminal domain and the RGS protein Ggamma-like domain.
5. The binding of RGS proteins to Galpha subunits is specific and depends on the type of RGS protein and the Galpha subunit involved.
6. The release of RGS proteins from Galpha subunits allows the activation of downstream signaling pathways, such as the Ras/ERK pathway, by the activated Galpha subunit.
7. The specificity of RGS-Galpha interactions is crucial for proper signaling regulation, as misregulation can lead to diseases such as cancer and metabolic disorders.

Overall, the mechanism of RGS-Galpha-based signaling involves a complex interplay between Gproteins, GPCRs, and RGS proteins, with specific interactions mediating the regulation of downstream signaling pathways.

Sensors function by detecting and measuring changes in physical properties such as light, temperature, pressure, or motion, converting these variations into electrical signals. This conversion process typically involves several components. First, the sensor's sensing element interacts with the physical phenomenon it's designed to detect. For instance, in a temperature sensor, a change in temperature alters the resistance of a thermistor or the voltage of a thermocouple. 

Next, signal conditioning circuits amplify, filter, or otherwise process the raw sensor output to improve accuracy and reliability. Analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) then convert the conditioned analog signal into a digital format suitable for processing by a microcontroller or other digital systems. Finally, the processed data is analyzed and interpreted by the system to make decisions or trigger actions based on the sensed information. This mechanism enables sensors to serve various functions across diverse applications, from environmental monitoring to industrial automation and beyond.

G protein activation involves a series of sequential steps initiated by the binding of an extracellular ligand to a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) embedded in the cell membrane. Upon ligand binding, the GPCR undergoes conformational changes, facilitating the exchange of GDP (guanosine diphosphate) bound to the G protein for GTP (guanosine triphosphate). This step is catalyzed by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs).

Once GTP is bound, the G protein dissociates into its active _-subunit and a __-subunit complex. Both subunits can interact with downstream effector molecules to initiate signaling cascades. The _-subunit activates or inhibits effector proteins such as enzymes or ion channels, modulating cellular responses. Meanwhile, the __-subunit complex can also regulate downstream effectors independently or in coordination with the _-subunit.

Following activation, the G protein signaling is terminated through the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP, facilitated by the intrinsic GTPase activity of the _-subunit. This hydrolysis restores the inactive GDP-bound state of the G protein, allowing it to reassociate with the GPCR and terminate the signaling cascade until the next ligand binding event. This sequential activation and deactivation cycle underpin the dynamic regulation of G protein-mediated cellular responses.

During G protein activation, a critical event occurs when the guanosine diphosphate (GDP) on the GÎ± subunit of G heterotrimers exchanges for guanosine triphosphate (GTP), which leads to the deactivation of GÎ±-GDP and the activation of GÎ±-GTP. This exchange is catalyzed by the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity of ligand-activated GPCRs. As a result, GÎ±-GTP and GÎ²Î³ dissociate or rearrange, allowing both to become active signaling species competent for engaging their respective effectors. The specific signaling pathways modulated by GÎ± subunits depend on the G-protein family to which they belong. GPCRs exhibit clear preferences for activating particular G proteins, and there has been tremendous progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying this selectivity. In light of the newest findings, GPCR and G protein activation is rather a coordinated, not sequential, process. Additionally, the opposing process of G protein deactivation occurs when G proteins hydrolyze guanosine triphosphate (GTP), a process assisted by the action of GAPs, which are essential for avoiding response saturation and achieving temporal resolution dictated by individual physiological reactions. Most well-characterized GAPs for heterotrimeric G proteins belong to the regulator of G protein signaling (RGS) family.

Several technologies have been employed to measure G protein activation, providing insights into the dynamics of signal transduction mediated by G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Various biophysical methods enable researchers to explore these intricate signaling pathways with high precision. One common approach involves radioligand binding assays, where the binding of a radiolabeled ligand to the GPCR is measured as a proxy for receptor activation. This technique offers high sensitivity and specificity but requires specialized equipment and safety precautions due to the use of radioactive compounds.  Another widely used method is fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), which detects changes in the proximity or conformation of fluorophore-labeled G proteins and GPCRs upon activation. FRET enables real-time monitoring of G protein activation dynamics in live cells with high spatiotemporal resolution. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) is similar to FRET but relies on the emission of bioluminescent light from luciferase-labeled proteins instead of fluorescence. BRET assays offer advantages such as minimal background signal and compatibility with high-throughput screening. More recently, biosensor technologies based on genetically encoded fluorescent or luminescent proteins have emerged, allowing direct visualization and quantification of G protein activation in live cells. These biosensors offer versatile tools for studying GPCR signaling in physiological contexts and drug discovery efforts.

Overall, GPCR-related gene transcription involves a complex interplay of signaling molecules and transcriptional regulators, orchestrating cellular responses to extracellular stimuli mediated by GPCRs.

Chemical proteomics, while a powerful approach, is not infallible due to several limitations:

1. Target Identification Bias: Chemical probes may exhibit preferential binding towards certain protein targets, leading to biased identification and incomplete coverage of the proteome.

2. Off-Target Effects: Chemical probes can interact with unintended protein targets, resulting in false-positive identifications and misinterpretation of results.

3. Dynamic Proteome: The proteome is dynamic and context-dependent, with protein expression, localization, and interactions varying across cell types, tissues, and conditions. Chemical proteomics may not capture this complexity comprehensively.

4. Limitations in Probe Design: The design and specificity of chemical probes influence their efficacy and selectivity. Imperfect probe design can lead to false interpretations and misassignment of protein targets.

5. Data Analysis Challenges: Chemical proteomics generates large datasets requiring sophisticated computational analyses for target identification and validation. Data interpretation may be complex and prone to errors or biases.

While chemical proteomics offers valuable insights into protein-ligand interactions and target identification, careful consideration of its limitations is essential to ensure accurate and reliable results. Integrating complementary approaches and rigorous validation strategies can enhance the robustness and reliability of chemical proteomics findings.

In the paper "Redefining the Protein Kinase Conformational Space with Machine Learning," the authors identify and describe several kinase conformations:

Active Conformation (CIDI - Catalytically Important DFG-in): This conformation is characterized by a high degree of catalytic activity, where the kinase is capable of binding and phosphorylating substrates. The DFG motif is in the "in" position, facilitating substrate binding and catalysis.

Inactive Conformation (CIDO - Catalytically Inactive DFG-out): This conformation lacks catalytic activity as the kinase is unable to bind or phosphorylate substrates. The DFG motif is in the "out" position, destabilizing ATP binding and preventing catalytic activity.

DFG-out Conformation (CODI - DFG-out): In this conformation, the DFG motif is flipped out, leading to an inactive state where ATP binding is hindered.

DFG-in Conformation (CODO - DFG-in): Here, the DFG motif is flipped in, facilitating ATP binding and stabilizing the active conformation of the kinase.

Unstable Conformation (uCD - Unstable Conformation): This conformation represents unstable or rarely populated states between active and inactive conformations, which may include partial unfolding or structural transitions.

The authors utilize machine learning algorithms to classify kinase structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) into these conformational states based on structural features such as the position of the DFG motif and the conformation of the Î±C helix. Understanding these conformations aids in identifying chemical substructures associated with each state, which can guide the development of conformation-specific kinase inhibitors.

The Foldseek workflow involves a systematic process for searching and comparing protein structures using a combination of structural and sequence-based approaches. Here's an explanation of each step:

Discretization of Structures: Both query and target protein structures are discretized into sequences of 3D interactions (3Di). This discretization process involves representing the interactions between residues within the protein structure in a simplified format suitable for computational analysis.

Prefiltering with MMseqs2: To efficiently detect candidate structures, a prefiltering step is applied using MMseqs2, a fast and sensitive tool for sequence comparison. This step involves using k-mer and ungapped alignment techniques on the 3Di sequences to identify potential matches between query and target structures.

Vectorized Smith-Waterman Alignment: Following the prefiltering step, a vectorized Smith-Waterman local alignment algorithm is employed. This algorithm combines the 3Di sequences with amino acid substitution scores to perform a detailed comparison between query and target structures. This comparison helps identify regions of structural similarity or homology between the two protein structures.

Global Alignment with TM-align: Alternatively, a global alignment approach is used, utilizing an accelerated version of TM-align. TM-align is a structural alignment algorithm that compares the overall fold of protein structures by superimposing their backbone atoms. This step provides a broader comparison of the overall structural similarity between query and target structures.

Learning the 3Di Alphabet: The 3Di alphabet is learned to describe the tertiary interactions between residues within protein structures. This process involves defining states based on the interaction geometry of residues and extracting relevant features such as angles, distances, and sequence information. These features are used to train a modified version of a Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to learn the most evolutionarily conserved 3Di states.

Prediction of Matching 3Di States: During structure searches, the trained encoder predicts the best-matching 3Di state for each residue in the protein structure. This prediction helps identify structurally similar regions between query and target structures, facilitating the comparison and alignment of protein folds.

Overall, the Foldseek workflow combines sequence-based prefiltering, detailed structural comparison, and machine learning techniques to efficiently search and align protein structures, enabling the discovery of structural similarities and homologies across diverse protein families.

Graph Attention Networks (GATs) address the algorithmic bottleneck of effectively modeling complex relationships within graph-structured data. Traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) struggle to capture long-range dependencies and varying importance levels of different nodes within a graph. This limitation arises due to the uniform treatment of neighboring nodes in the aggregation process.

GATs introduce the concept of attention mechanisms, inspired by mechanisms used in sequence-to-sequence models in natural language processing. By incorporating attention mechanisms, GATs can selectively attend to relevant nodes in the neighborhood while assigning varying importance weights to them. This allows GATs to effectively capture the intricate structural information present in graphs.

The attention mechanism in GATs enables nodes to dynamically adjust their contributions to the representation of a target node based on their importance, thus overcoming the uniformity constraint of traditional GNNs. Consequently, GATs offer improved performance in tasks such as node classification, graph classification, and link prediction, making them particularly well-suited for scenarios where capturing complex graph structures is crucial.

Transductive and inductive tasks in the context of graph neural networks (GNNs) differ in their approaches to handling data and making predictions. In transductive tasks, the model aims to predict labels or properties for nodes or edges within a known graph structure. This means that the model is trained on a specific graph and makes predictions only for the nodes or edges present in that graph. It does not generalize to unseen nodes or graphs. Transductive tasks focus on exploiting the existing graph structure to make predictions accurately within that structure.

On the other hand, in inductive tasks, the model is trained on a particular graph but aims to generalize its predictions to unseen nodes or graphs that may have different structures. This means that the model learns underlying patterns from the training graph and applies them to make predictions on new, unseen graphs or nodes. Inductive tasks require models to capture more generalizable features and structural patterns from the training data.

Overall, transductive tasks focus on making predictions within a specific graph structure, while inductive tasks aim to generalize predictions to unseen data or structures beyond the training set.

In graph neural networks (GNNs), the GAT (Graph Attention Network) mechanism is a key component that enables the model to selectively focus on certain parts of the graph. The GAT mechanism consists of the following individual steps:

1. Graph embedding: Each node in the graph is represented as a dense vector in a high-dimensional space.
2. Attention scoring: For each node, an attention score is computed based on the similarity between its own embedding and the embeddings of neighboring nodes.
3. Weighted aggregation: The attention scores are used to weight the contributions of each node to the output, resulting in a weighted sum of the node representations.
4. Non-linear transformation: The weighted sum is passed through a non-linear activation function to produce the final node representation.
5. Repeat for all nodes in the graph: Steps 1-4 are repeated for each node in the graph, allowing the model to capture complex patterns and relationships between nodes.

The EFFECT benchmark suite is a specialized tool designed to evaluate the performance of machine learning models in predicting both cancer vulnerabilities and drug responses. It leverages datasets such as DepMap and GDSC, which encompass information on gene essentiality and drug sensitivity in various cancer cell lines. This comprehensive approach enables researchers to develop models that accurately forecast the importance of genes and the efficacy of drugs across different cancer types. By bridging the gap between theoretical models and practical applications in drug discovery, EFFECT plays a crucial role in advancing personalized medicine strategies tailored to individual patient needs.

The EFFECT benchmark suite controls for dataset biases when evaluating cancer dependency predictors by using cell line/perturbation exclusive data splits, perturbation-wise evaluation, and the application of a Bias Detector framework. The Bias Detector can identify model predictions not explicable by data bias alone, which helps to reduce the effects of data biases in the performance evaluation. Additionally, the authors applied DeepDEP with full genomic input to the TCGA data to predict the dependency profiles of 1298 DepOIs in 8238 tumors and found similar distributions of predicted dependency scores as the original and predicted dependency scores of CCLs. Overall, the EFFECT benchmark suite aims to provide a unified test and evaluation pipeline for machine learning models predicting cancer sensitivity data, facilitating unbiased benchmarking to support teams in improving on the state of the art.

The authors of the EFFECT benchmark suite suggest using the following practical guideline to critically evaluate machine learning (ML) models: "Evaluate the model on a held-out test set, rather than relying solely on cross-validation within the training set and use multiple source for hold-out sets." This helps to ensure that the model is generalizing well to new, unseen data and is not overfitting to the training set.

Confounding biases present in cancer dependency datasets include:

1. Selection bias: Sampling bias can occur when the sample of patients is not representative of the population of interest. For example, if a study only includes patients from a specific hospital or region, it may not be generalizable to other populations.
2. Information bias: The quality and completeness of the data can affect the accuracy of the prediction methods. For example, if the dataset is missing important variables or has incorrect values, the predictions may not be accurate.
3. Measurement bias: Variables in the dataset may be measured with errors or inconsistencies, which can influence the predictions. For example, if the tumor size is measured using different methods, it may lead to different predictions.
4. Time bias: The timing of the data collection and analysis can affect the results. For example, if the study is conducted at a specific time point after treatment, it may not capture the full range of changes that occur over time.
5. Funding bias: Studies that are funded by organizations with a vested interest in the outcome may be more likely to report biased results.

These confounding biases can influence objective comparison of prediction methods by leading to inaccurate or misleading results. For example, if a study is conducted with a biased sample or incomplete data, it may overestimate the accuracy of a particular prediction method, while another study with better quality data may find different results. Therefore, it is important to carefully consider these potential biases when comparing prediction methods and interpreting the results.

Predicting cancer dependencies from DepMap data, a massive resource on gene essentiality in cancer cell lines, is a hot area with several advanced machine learning methods:

* **Deep Learning:** Techniques like DeepDEP leverage deep neural networks to analyze complex relationships between gene expression and essentiality scores. This allows them to capture non-linear patterns and potentially discover new dependencies.

* **Graph Neural Networks (GNNs):** These models treat DepMap data as a network of genes and interactions. GNNs like GAT can learn from the network structure, considering not just individual genes but how they interact with others, leading to more comprehensive dependency predictions.

* **Ensemble Methods:** Combining predictions from multiple algorithms (e.g., random forests and support vector machines) can improve accuracy and reduce bias.  

However, a major challenge is  **dataset bias**. Cancer cell lines may not perfectly reflect real tumors, and factors like drug promiscuity can skew results. The EFFECT benchmark suite helps address this by controlling for bias and enabling fairer evaluation of these powerful machine learning methods.

Overall, the field is rapidly evolving, with researchers constantly refining methods to extract the most reliable cancer dependency insights from DepMap data.

While research is ongoing, there isn't a definitive consensus on SSS having overall advantages over transformers. Here's a breakdown of potential benefits:

* **Efficiency:**  SSS architectures might require  **fewer parameters** compared to transformers for similar performance. This translates to faster training times and potentially lower computational resources needed.

* **Interpretability:**  SSS utilizes simpler mechanisms for capturing relationships between data points. This can make it easier to understand how the model arrives at its predictions, offering valuable insights into the underlying data patterns.

However, transformers boast their own strengths:

* **Parallelization:** Their structure allows for efficient  **parallel processing**, making them suitable for leveraging powerful computing hardware for faster training.

* **Long-range dependencies:** Transformers excel at capturing relationships between distant elements in data sequences, which can be crucial for tasks like natural language processing.

Overall, the choice between SSS and transformers depends on the specific application and its priorities. SSS might be preferred for efficiency and interpretability, while transformers might be better suited for tasks that demand strong long-range dependency modeling and can benefit from parallel processing.

RNA-seq profiles can differ significantly between patient-derived cancer samples and samples from cell lines like those in the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) due to several factors:

1. Tissue Heterogeneity: Patient-derived cancer samples often consist of a mix of cancer cells, stromal cells, immune cells, and other cell types present in the tumor microenvironment. In contrast, cell lines in CCLE typically comprise homogeneous populations of cancer cells. This tissue heterogeneity can lead to differences in gene expression profiles between patient samples and cell lines.

2. Genetic Variation: Patient-derived cancer samples may exhibit genetic mutations, copy number variations, and epigenetic alterations that are absent in cell lines. These genetic differences can influence gene expression patterns and contribute to divergent RNA-seq profiles between patient samples and cell lines.

3. In Vitro Culture Conditions: Cell lines in CCLE are often cultured in artificial in vitro conditions, which can induce changes in gene expression compared to the in vivo tumor microenvironment experienced by patient samples. This includes alterations in nutrient availability, oxygen levels, and growth factor signaling, leading to differences in RNA-seq profiles.

Overall, the interplay of tissue heterogeneity, genetic variation, and in vitro culture conditions contributes to the observed differences in RNA-seq profiles between patient-derived cancer samples and CCLE samples.

The results obtained from Celligner allow researchers to analyze the organization of cancer subtypes in several ways:

1. Conserved Cell Types: Celligner identifies cell types that are conserved across different cancer subtypes, providing insights into the cellular composition and heterogeneity of tumors.

2. Differential Expression Analysis: By comparing gene expression profiles between conserved cell types across cancer subtypes, Celligner enables the identification of subtype-specific gene expression signatures associated with different cancer subtypes.

3. Clustering and Visualization: Celligner allows for clustering and visualization of cells based on their gene expression profiles, enabling researchers to explore the organization of cancer subtypes in multidimensional gene expression space.

Overall, Celligner results provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing cancer subtype organization by identifying conserved cell types and gene expression patterns across different cancer subtypes, thus enhancing our understanding of tumor heterogeneity and facilitating the discovery of subtype-specific biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Masif, a tool for predicting protein-ligand binding affinity, has several weaknesses and limitations. Firstly, its reliance on 3D protein structures limits its applicability to cases where such structures are available, excluding proteins with unknown or difficult-to-determine structures. Additionally, the accuracy of Masif predictions can be affected by structural inaccuracies or errors in the input protein-ligand complexes.

To address these limitations, incorporating methods for predicting protein structures from sequence data could expand Masif's applicability to a wider range of proteins. Additionally, integrating information from multiple structural prediction tools and experimental datasets could enhance the accuracy of predicted protein structures.

Furthermore, to improve prediction accuracy, incorporating additional features such as protein dynamics, solvent accessibility, and ligand flexibility could provide a more comprehensive representation of protein-ligand interactions. Additionally, leveraging deep learning techniques and larger training datasets could enhance the predictive power of Masif by capturing more complex relationships between protein and ligand features.

Overall, addressing these weaknesses through advancements in structural prediction, feature representation, and machine learning methods could enhance the capabilities and accuracy of Masif for predicting protein-ligand binding affinity.

According to the provided information, Masif compares favorably to other state-of-the-art methods for large-scale docking. Masif achieved performances similar to PatchDock but with much faster CPU time, taking only four central processing unit (CPU) minutes compared to PatchDock's 2,743 CPU minutes. Additionally, when MaSIF-search was run with only 100 decoys per target, its performance was comparable to PatchDock.

2. Fingerprinting: Patterns of chemical and geometric features are deciphered to reveal information about protein interactions with other biomolecules.
3. Geometric deep learning method: A general method based on geometric deep learning recognizes and decodes patterns on the molecular surface without considering the underlying protein sequence or structural fold.
4. Prediction challenges: MASIF is applied to three prediction challenges: protein pocket-ligand prediction, proteinï¿½protein interaction site prediction, and ultrafast scanning of protein surfaces for prediction of proteinï¿½protein complexes.

Deploying a prediction model trained on Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) data to cancer-derived patient samples presents several challenges:

1. Biological Variability: Patient-derived samples exhibit greater biological variability compared to cell lines, reflecting diverse genetic backgrounds, tumor microenvironments, and disease states. The model may not generalize well to these variations, leading to reduced predictive performance.

2. Dataset Shift: Differences in experimental protocols, sequencing platforms, and data preprocessing methods between CCLE and patient-derived datasets can introduce dataset shift, causing discrepancies in data distributions. This can hinder the model's ability to generalize to new data.

3. Limited Sample Size: Patient-derived datasets often have smaller sample sizes compared to CCLE, increasing the risk of overfitting and limiting the model's ability to capture diverse biological patterns.

4. Ethical and Regulatory Considerations: Deploying models trained on CCLE data to patient samples raises ethical and regulatory concerns regarding patient privacy, data sharing, and informed consent, which must be addressed to ensure compliance with legal and ethical standards.

Addressing these challenges requires robust validation strategies, careful consideration of dataset biases, and rigorous evaluation of model performance on patient-derived samples to ensure reliable and clinically relevant predictions.

Linkers can have a significant impact on protein folding and stability. Several studies have shown that the choice of linker can influence the folding and stability of proteins, particularly when linking multiple domains. Here are some key findings:

1. Protein/CAR stability: Linkers can help stabilize protein structures by providing additional hydrophilic interactions and reducing the exposure of hydrophobic regions to the solvent. For example, a study by Argos (1990) found that the use of small, non-polar linkers increased the stability of gene fusion proteins.
2. Folding: The length and structure of the linker can affect the folding of the protein. Short, flexible linkers can facilitate the folding of the protein by providing a pathway for the polypeptide chain to follow during translation (Chen et al., 2013). On the other hand, long, rigid linkers can hinder folding by creating barriers or steric clashes with the surrounding domains.
3. Aggregation: The properties of the linker can influence protein aggregation. For instance, Chen et al. (2013) found that flexible linkers inhibited protein aggregation, while rigid linkers promoted it. This is because flexible linkers allow for more conformational flexibility, reducing the likelihood of steric clashes and promoting proper folding, while rigid linkers can create a more stable structure, leading to increased aggregation.
4. Expression: The choice of linker can also impact protein expression. For example, Evers et al. (2006) found that the addition of polar residues in the linker reduced protein expression by disrupting the folding of the flanking domains. This suggests that linkers with non-polar or small hydrophilic residues may be more suitable for expression purposes.

In summary, the properties of the linker can significantly impact protein folding, stability, aggregation, and expression. The choice of linker depends on the specific application, and a thorough understanding of the relationship between linkers and protein structure is crucial for designing effective linkers in gene fusion proteins.

CAR (Chimeric Antigen Receptor) therapy has shown remarkable success in treating certain cancers, but it also faces limitations. One significant challenge is antigen escape, where cancer cells mutate or downregulate the targeted antigen, leading to treatment resistance. Additionally, off-target toxicity poses risks, where CAR T cells attack healthy tissues expressing the target antigen at low levels. Another concern is the tumor microenvironment's immunosuppressive nature, hindering CAR T cell function and persistence.

To overcome these limitations, researchers are exploring various strategies. One approach involves targeting multiple antigens simultaneously, reducing the likelihood of antigen escape. They're also designing safer CAR constructs with enhanced tumor specificity and reduced off-target effects, employing methods such as incorporating safety switches or utilizing tissue-specific promoters. Furthermore, modifying CAR T cells to resist immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment, such as adding cytokine receptors or disrupting inhibitory signaling pathways, aims to improve their efficacy. Additionally, combinatorial therapies, like combining CAR T cells with checkpoint inhibitors or other immunomodulatory agents, are being investigated to enhance treatment outcomes. These innovative strategies hold promise in advancing CAR therapy to address its limitations and improve its effectiveness in cancer treatment.

According to the review, there are currently no CAR therapies approved for treating solid tumors. One of the challenges in designing CARs for solid tumors is the diverse nature of these cancers, which can express different antigens and have varying levels of expression. This makes it difficult to identify a single target antigen that can be effectively targeted by a CAR T cell. Additionally, solid tumors often have a complex microenvironment that can impede the activity of CAR T cells, such as immune suppressive cells and the presence of tumor-associated macrophages. These factors make it challenging to overcome treatment resistance and achieve long-lasting responses with CAR T cell therapy in solid tumors.

A Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) is a synthetic receptor engineered to be expressed on the surface of T cells, a type of immune cell. It's designed to recognize specific proteins, known as antigens, found on the surface of cancer cells or infected cells. CARs are composed of several components, including an extracellular antigen-binding domain, a transmembrane domain, and one or more intracellular signaling domains.

The extracellular domain typically consists of a single-chain variable fragment (scFv), derived from an antibody, which determines the CAR's specificity for the target antigen. The transmembrane domain anchors the CAR to the T cell membrane, while the intracellular signaling domains, such as those derived from T cell receptor (TCR) signaling molecules and co-stimulatory molecules, activate the T cell upon antigen binding, leading to the destruction of the target cell.

CAR T cell therapy involves genetically modifying a patient's own T cells to express CARs, enabling them to recognize and attack cancer cells or infected cells more effectively. This personalized immunotherapy approach has shown significant promise in treating certain types of cancer and other diseases by harnessing the power of the immune system.

There are several viral transduction methods that have been used to introduce genetic material into T-cells to generate CAR-T cells. These include:

1. Retroviruses: Retroviruses, such as murine leukemia virus (MLV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), have been widely used for gene transfer into T-cells.
2. Lentiviruses: Lentiviruses, such as HIV, can also be used for gene transfer into T-cells.
3. Adenoviruses: Adenoviruses are small, double-stranded DNA viruses that have been used to deliver genetic material into T-cells.
4. Herpesviruses: Herpesviruses, such as glycoprotein B (GPCR) of herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1), have been engineered to express CAR and used for gene transfer into T-cells.
5. AAV vectors: Adeno-associated viruses (AAV) are small, single-stranded DNA viruses that have been used for gene transfer into T-cells.
6. BCM-like retroviruses: Bovine cathepsin M (BCM)-like retroviruses are a new class of retroviruses that have been developed for gene transfer into T-cells.
7. Minicell vectors: Minicell vectors are small, non-pathogenic viruses that have been used for gene transfer into T-cells.
8. Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs): LNPs are non-viral particles that can be used to deliver genetic material into T-cells.
9. Electroporation: Electroporation is a method of introducing genetic material into cells using an electric pulse. It has been used for gene transfer into T-cells.
10. Magnetofection: Magnetofection is a method of introducing genetic material into cells using a magnetic field. It has been used for gene transfer into T-cells.

There are several promising CAR-T designs that go beyond monospecific constructs, including:

1. Bispecific CAR-T cells: These cells are engineered to express two different CARs on their surface, allowing them to recognize and target multiple cancer antigens simultaneously.
2. Dual-specificity CAR-T cells: These cells are designed to recognize and target two different types of cancer antigens, providing a more comprehensive approach to cancer therapy.
3. Multi-specific CAR-T cells: These cells are engineered to express multiple CARs on their surface, allowing them to recognize and target multiple cancer antigens simultaneously.
4. T-cell receptor (TCR) CAR-T cells: These cells are engineered to express a TCR in addition to a CAR, providing a more diverse and adaptive immune response against cancer.
5. Combination CAR-T cells: These cells are engineered to express multiple CARs on their surface, as well as other therapeutic molecules such as cytokines or chemokines, allowing for a more targeted and effective therapy.

The development of better Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapies faces several challenges, ranked in order of difficulty as follows:

1. Persistence and long-term survival of CAR-T cells: Despite their potent anti-tumor activity, CAR-T cells are often short-lived, leading to limited durability and efficacy. Strategies to overcome this challenge include the use of bone marrow stromal cells to enhance CAR-T cell survival [1], or the development of new CAR structures that promote CAR-T cell longevity [2].

2. Managing toxicities: CAR-T cell therapy can cause severe side effects, such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity. Approaches to mitigate these adverse events include the use of immune suppressive drugs [3], or the development of strategies to reduce CAR-T cell activation and proliferation [4].

3. Targeting tumor antigen heterogeneity: Cancer cells often express multiple tumor antigens, which can limit the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy. Techniques to address this challenge include the use of multi-antigenic CARs [5], or the development of strategies to selectively target specific tumor antigens [6].

4. Overcoming immune resistance: Cancer cells can evade the immune system by suppressing immune activation or activating regulatory T cells (Tregs). Strategies to overcome these mechanisms include the use of drugs that inhibit Treg function [7], or the development of CAR-T cell therapies that target multiple immune checkpoints simultaneously [8].

5. Cost and accessibility: CAR-T cell therapy is expensive and not widely available, limiting access for many patients. Strategies to address this challenge include the development of more cost-effective production processes [9], or the use of off-the-shelf CAR-T cells that can be readily available for patients [10].

In summary, the biggest issues facing the development of better CAR-T therapies are persistence and long-term survival, managing toxicities, targeting tumor antigen heterogeneity, overcoming immune resistance, and cost and accessibility. Addressing these challenges will require a combination of innovative strategies and technologies to improve CAR-T cell therapy outcomes.

The composition of the hinge region in CARs can affect its efficiency of signal transduction in several ways:

1. Flexibility: The hinge region provides flexibility to overcome steric hindrance and contributes to the length of the CAR to allow the antigen-binding domain to access the targeted epitope. A longer hinge region can provide more flexibility, which can improve the efficiency of signal transduction by allowing the CAR to bind to a wider range of antigens.
2. Spacer length: The position of the epitope and its distance to the cell surface are expected to affect the binding to the antigen and the optimal formation of T-cell target conjugates and synapses. A shorter spacer length can lead to a higher density of CARs on the T-cell membrane, which can improve signal transduction efficiency.
3. Distance from the cell surface: The distance between the epitope and the cell surface can also affect the binding affinity and specificity of the CAR. A shorter hinge region can lead to a closer proximity of the epitope to the cell surface, which can improve signal transduction efficiency by reducing the distance between the CAR and the antigen.
4. Afferent signaling: The composition of the hinge region can also affect afferent signaling, or the ability of the CAR to transmit signals from the antigen to the T cell. A longer hinge region can provide more time for afferent signaling, leading to improved efficiency of signal transduction.
5. Epitope recognition: The composition of the hinge region can also affect epitope recognition by providing more flexibility and allowing the CAR to bind to a wider range of antigens. A longer hinge region can provide more options for epitope recognition, leading to improved efficiency of signal transduction.

In summary, the composition of the hinge region in CARs can affect its efficiency of signal transduction by providing flexibility, reducing distance from the cell surface, improving afferent signaling, and increasing epitope recognition options.
